title: Agni Loses His Appetite
hook: Agni falls sick from too much ghee; the Gita says that same fire lives in every body, so a meal is an offering, fed well in winter
carry: eating is an offering to the fire within
tomorrow: why does spring ask you to go lighter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma waited for the sun: the sun's turn north is held sacred, and the year has a taking half and a giving half.

Agni, the god of fire, is sick. A king named Shvetaki has spent years pouring ghee into sacrificial fires, and Agni has had to take in all of it. Now he's pale, sluggish, and he's lost his appetite. Fire, off his food. So he goes to Brahma, the creator, and asks what's wrong with him.
screen: `AGNI IS SICK.` → `YEARS OF GHEE.` → `FIRE, OFF HIS FOOD.`

segments.voice: This is from the Mahabharata's first book. Brahma's answer is a change of diet: the right fuel will restore you. Agni's cure comes at a fierce cost, the burning of the Khandava forest, with Krishna and Arjuna helping him, and the epic doesn't hide how terrible that fire is. But hold on to the picture at the start: fire can be overfed, and fire can be hungry. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, the fire that digests your food is Agni too. In the Gita, Krishna says: I become Vaishvanara, the fire in the bodies of living beings, and joined with the breath, I digest the food. So eating is an offering into a sacred fire. That's why many Hindus say a Gita verse before meals, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Ayurveda builds its seasons around the same fire. The Charaka Samhita says that in the cold months, hemanta and shishira, the inner fire is held in by the cold and grows strong, and needs warm, substantial food. Starve it, the text warns, and it turns on the body's own tissues. And at Makar Sankranti in midwinter, families give each other sesame and jaggery: winter food, shared. Today, a bigger appetite on a cold day isn't a failing to fight; on this teaching it's a fire doing its work. And any meal can be offered before it's eaten. Many Christians say grace, thanking God for the food; the Hindu verse goes on to call the eating itself worship.
screen: `AGNI'S CURE: THE RIGHT FUEL` · `VAISHVANARA: THE FIRE WITHIN` · `WINTER'S FIRE IS STRONG` · `ANY MEAL CAN BE OFFERED`

segments.voice: Find the warmest place in the body right now, the chest or the belly, and rest your attention there, feeling the out-breath warm as it leaves. Then picture your next meal. Many Hindus fold their hands before eating and say brahmarpanam, offering the food first; if you pray, you can try that at your next meal, and if you don't, take one breath of thanks before the first bite.
The seasons. In winter, Charaka reads a strong inner fire held in by the cold; the Gita calls that fire Vaishvanara, God in the body.
Your line: eating is an offering to the fire within. Agni, fed well. Until tomorrow.
